# Hydraulic ram (`hydraulic_ram`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by piston_pump, blast_furnace_cast_iron
- Core idea: A pump with no engine and two moving parts. Water runs from a stream down a long, rigid iron drive pipe and spills out through a weighted waste valve at the bottom. As the flow speeds up it slams the waste valve shut; the moving column of water cannot stop at once, and the pressure shock forces a little water through a second one-way valve into an air vessel and up a delivery pipe to many times the height of the fall. The pressure then drops, the waste valve falls open and the cycle repeats about once a second. With a fall of 1 m it lifts roughly one fifteenth of the water to 10 m; the rest is the price paid.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calling it perpetual motion; it wastes nine tenths of the water to lift one tenth
  - A short, soft or leaky drive pipe (wood, lead, hose) that swallows the shock
  - No air vessel, or one that has filled with water: the pipe hammers itself apart
  - Expecting it to work without a fall of at least half a metre and a steady flow
- History: europe: 1772 – John Whitehurst's hand-operated pulsation engine at Oulton, Cheshire; 1796 Joseph-Michel Montgolfier makes it self-acting (French patent 1797); americas: 1809 – first United States patent (Cerneau and Hallet); common on farms from the 1840s; global: 20th c. – widely used for village water supply in hilly country
- Read:
  - John Whitehurst, Account of a Machine for Raising Water, Executed at Oulton, in Cheshire, in 1772, Phil. Trans. 65 (1775)
  - Joseph-Michel Montgolfier, Note sur le bélier hydraulique, et sur la manière d’en calculer les effets, Journal des mines 13, no. 73 (1802), 42–51
